title: Confidence intervals for empirical convergence rates of randomised quasi-Monte Carlo, with applications to option pricing
year_and_status: arXiv v1 24 Feb 2025; v2 16 Sep 2026 (barrier and preintegration material appears only in v2); preprint, no journal version established
what_it_does: Builds bootstrap/resampling confidence intervals for fitted RQMC convergence exponents. v2 Sec. 10 'Smoothing by preintegration', Table 8: a single-asset GBM arithmetic-Asian call with discrete up-and-out knock-out (B=130, m=64/121/256 dates) is preintegrated along the leading principal component (Newton+bisection root find for the knock-out threshold). The exponent moves only from about -0.54 to -0.55/-0.56, while the error falls 6-9x through the constant. The same conditioning moves a digital Asian from about -0.58 to about -1.06/-1.07. Sec. 10 explains the failure: after conditioning, the knock-out threshold is a minimum over dates and has kinks where the binding date changes. Table 7 also gives plain-RQMC barrier exponents of about -0.50 to -0.55 under incremental, bridge and PCA constructions. Tables 9/11-12 (5-asset baskets) contain no knock-out payoff.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the closest published precedent for C2 and partially pre-empts its qualitative message: preintegration restores about n^-1 for a digital but not for a discretely monitored knock-out, with the same mechanism. Its limits: single asset only (d=1), one smoother (first-PC preintegration), no one-step-survival conditioning (Glasserman-Staum), no multi-direction numerical smoothing, no multi-asset basket barrier and no timing-to-accuracy. C2's defensible residual novelty is therefore: multi-asset basket knock-outs at 48/416 dimensions, two different smoothers (first-PC preintegration and one-step survival) both measured at about 0.48-0.63, bootstrap intervals, and use of the rate inside a quantum requirements frontier. C2 wording must cite Case v2 Sec. 10 / Table 8 and must not claim to be the first to observe the knock-out rate failure. The repo already cites v2 (docs/research_investigation/2026-09-22/DECISION.md and qqmc_review.md) for slope diagnostics and Asian preintegration only; the barrier result in Sec. 10 was not recorded there. It is not in the four designated literature files.

title: Conditional sampling for barrier option pricing under the LT method
authors: Nico Achtsis, Ronald Cools, Dirk Nuyens
year_and_status: arXiv v1 21 Nov 2011, v2 27 Dec 2012; published SIAM J. Financial Math. 4(1):327-352 (2013), DOI 10.1137/110855909 (journal pages from search/citing text, not opened on the publisher site)
what_it_does: Combines Glasserman-Staum one-step-survival conditional sampling with the Imai-Tan LT path construction under randomized QMC (Sobol with digital shifts, and lattice; 4096 points x 40 shifts). It modifies the first uniform so the barrier asset survives every date, proves unbiasedness and no variance increase, extends to knock-ins (Sec. 6) and adds root-finding for payoff positivity (Sec. 7). Sec. 5.1 prices a 4-asset GBM arithmetic-Asian basket with an up-and-out barrier on asset 1 over m=130 dates (520 dimensions). Table 2 gives fitted std-dev exponents of 0.55-0.73 for QMC+LT+CS, 0.53-0.58 for QMC+LT and about 0.49-0.50 for MC+CS. The text says CS improves the rate in only two of four cases. Sec. 5.4 / Table 4 (single-asset binary barrier): both QMC rates fall as m grows, from about 1.18 (CS, m=2) to about 0.50 by m=60. The authors conclude that CS gives variance reduction, not necessarily a higher convergence rate. Sec. 7 root-finding gives further 2-7x std-dev reductions (Table 6), with no rate reported.
difference_from_our_paper: This pre-empts the core empirical content of C2 on a multi-asset, high-dimensional, discretely monitored knock-out: one-step-survival conditioning plus a dimension-reducing QMC construction gave 0.55-0.73, not n^-1, and the authors say so explicitly. C2 must cite it as the earliest evidence. Differences: their barrier is on a single asset (S1) inside a 4-asset basket, whereas ours is on the basket; 130 dates vs our 12/52; LT rather than PCA/bridge; no first-PC preintegration; no bootstrap intervals; no timing; no link to quantum budgets. Our measured 0.48-0.57 (one-step survival) and 0.53-0.63 (preintegration) are consistent with their Table 2. C2 is therefore 'known and confirmed on new shapes', not a new phenomenon. It is also not contradicted: nothing here restores near n^-1 for multi-date knock-outs. Not in the four designated files; Glasserman-Staum appears only in WHY_NO_ADVANTAGE.md refs.

title: An integrated quasi-Monte Carlo method for handling high dimensional problems with discontinuities in financial engineering
year_and_status: arXiv v1 8 Sep 2017, v2 26 Feb 2019; a journal version exists under DOI 10.1007/s10614-020-09976-2 (Springer, Computational Economics by DOI prefix; landing page not opened)
what_it_does: Proposes 'variable push-out' (VPO) smoothing, which it states generalizes the Achtsis et al. LT conditional-sampling idea, plus a modified QR path generation method, for RQMC on discontinuous payoffs under Black-Scholes, exponential NIG and Heston. Example 3 is a single-asset discretely monitored down-and-out call. Its best smoothed method gives VRF about 112 at d=16 but only about 15 at d=128 (Table 1, BS), and 206 at m=16 vs 30 at m=64 under NIG (Table 3). The authors say the barrier's m discontinuity structures and the cusps in the max over dates leave the smoothed integrand less smooth, so gains are 'moderate' and fall with dimension. Binary-Asian and Asian-delta examples reach VRFs in the thousands or more.
difference_from_our_paper: This independently confirms, for a single-asset discrete knock-out, the mechanism behind C2: conditioning removes one jump, but the max-over-dates boundary keeps cusps, so gains shrink as monitoring dates grow. It reports VRFs rather than fitted exponents, uses one asset, and gives no timing or quantum comparison. It does not restore near n^-1 for knock-outs, so it supports rather than contradicts C2. C2 should cite it next to Case v2 Sec. 10 and Achtsis et al. 2013 for the cusp mechanism. Not in the four designated files.

title: The smoothing effect of integration in R^d and the ANOVA decomposition (Math. Comp. 82:383-400, 2013), its Note (Math. Comp.), and 'The ANOVA decomposition of a non-smooth function of infinitely many variables can have every term smooth'
authors: Michael Griebel, Frances Y. Kuo, Ian H. Sloan
year_and_status: Math. Comp. 82 (2013) 383-400, citation taken from the authors' own reference list; the Note and the infinite-variable paper are Math. Comp. companions (journal volume/pages of these two not verified here). Author-hosted preprint of the infinite-variable paper read.
what_it_does: Theory for the 'kink' case: for f = max(phi,0) with phi smooth and suitably monotone in one Gaussian variable, integrating out that variable (the preintegration / ANOVA mechanism) gives smooth lower-order ANOVA terms. This explains why QMC and sparse grids work on Asian/basket calls despite the kink. The infinite-variable paper extends this to the continuous-path Brownian-bridge (Levy-Ciesielski) formulation. Its footnote records that the 2013 main theorem did not, as claimed, apply to the Asian option, and that the Note repairs this.
difference_from_our_paper: Provides the positive theory for the payoff classes where our smoothers work (calls, and digitals with a monotone direction). The analysed class is a single smooth function phi inside max(.,0). A discretely monitored knock-out multiplies the kink by an indicator of a minimum over monitoring dates, so it lies outside the theorems' hypotheses. This theory therefore neither predicts n^-1 for our knock-outs nor contradicts C2. Cite it as the reason calls/digitals recover and as why the knock-out is structurally different. Math. Comp. 2013 page not opened; only the infinite-variable preprint was read. Not in the four designated files.

title: High dimensional integration of kinks and jumps -- smoothing by preintegration
authors: Andreas Griewank, Frances Y. Kuo, Hernan Leovey, Ian H. Sloan
year_and_status: arXiv v1 4 Dec 2017; journal version reported elsewhere as J. Comput. Appl. Math. (2018), not verified on the publisher page
what_it_does: Rigorous preintegration theory for integrands of the form theta(x)*ind(phi(x)), covering kinks (theta=phi) and jumps such as digitals. The key assumption is that phi is smooth with a strictly positive partial derivative in one variable x_j (monotone), plus growth conditions. Then integrating out x_j gives a (d-1)-dimensional function in a mixed Sobolev space, so QMC and sparse grids apply. The worked example is a digital Asian with PCA. The intro states that 'conditional sampling' (Glasserman-Staum; Achtsis et al.) and root-finding smoothing are the same practical tool.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the theorem that predicts near n^-1 for our calls and digitals. For a discretely monitored knock-out, the survival event is ind(min over dates of (H - S_basket(t_i))). Its phi is a minimum of smooth functions, which is non-smooth even when it is monotone in the first PC, and it multiplies a second (strike) indicator. The theorem's smoothness hypothesis therefore fails, which gives the formal reason C2's knock-out result is expected rather than anomalous. No barrier example appears; it neither contradicts nor pre-empts C2 but should be cited as the hypothesis the knock-out violates. Not in the four designated files; the related 2112.11621 (non-monotone case) is already in the screening table.

title: Analysis of preintegration followed by quasi-Monte Carlo integration for distribution functions and densities
authors: Alexander D. Gilbert, Frances Y. Kuo, Ian H. Sloan
year_and_status: arXiv v1 20 Dec 2021, v5 6 Oct 2022; published SIAM J. Numer. Anal. (2023), DOI 10.1137/21M146658X (DOI from search listing; publisher page not opened)
what_it_does: Proves that preintegration along a suitably chosen variable, followed by QMC, estimates CDFs and densities of X = phi(x) at nearly first-order rates in weighted spaces, under a monotonicity assumption in the preintegration variable. Appendix A.3 shows that monotonicity is necessary: without it the preintegrated function has singularities. The worked example is an Asian option value. It cites Glasserman-Staum and Achtsis et al. as the conditional-sampling antecedents.
difference_from_our_paper: Supplies the near-n^-1 guarantee for single-threshold events (digitals, distribution functions) that our calls and digitals achieve. It does not treat multi-date knock-outs, whose survival boundary is a minimum over dates. It is theory support for the 'calls/digitals recover' half of C2 and silent on the knock-out half. Not in the four designated files; the companion 2112.11621 and 2212.11493 are already screened.

title: Conditioning on One-Step Survival for Barrier Option Simulations
year_and_status: Operations Research 49(6):923-937 (2001). The publisher page returned 403. The author preprint (June 1999, revised December 1999) was read in full via CiteSeerX (https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.32.7666&rep=rep1&type=pdf).
what_it_does: Introduces the one-step-survival estimator. Each monitoring step is sampled conditional on not crossing the barrier, and the payoff is weighted by the product of one-step survival probabilities (a likelihood ratio). This is an unbiased change of measure with provably no more variance than standard MC. When the conditional laws are unknown, it adds estimated-likelihood-ratio variants. Numerics are plain Monte Carlo only (no QMC): single-stock single/double barriers, a stock-plus-index example with barriers on the index, and LIBOR-market-model barrier swaptions with 3-12 monitoring dates. Work x variance gains are large when knock-out probability is high. Table 5 shows the efficiency gain of the exact estimator falling as the number of monitoring dates grows (binary double barrier, m=1..60).
difference_from_our_paper: This is the origin of the 'one-step survival' smoother used in our P3 arm, so C2 must cite it as the method source. It is an MC variance-reduction paper: it makes no convergence-rate or QMC claim, so it neither pre-empts nor contradicts C2's RQMC exponent finding. Its Table 5 observation that per-date conditioning loses efficiency as monitoring dates grow is a qualitative precursor of our 12- vs 52-date behaviour. Not in the four designated files; listed only in WHY_NO_ADVANTAGE.md Sec. 10 without a URL.

title: An importance sampling-based smoothing approach for quasi-Monte Carlo simulation of discrete barrier options
authors: Fei Xie, Zhijian He, Xiaoqun Wang
year_and_status: European Journal of Operational Research 274(2):759-772 (16 Apr 2019), per search-engine metadata. The publisher page returned HTTP 403; no arXiv or author copy found.
what_it_does: According to the abstract text in search snippets, not read on the primary page: a sequential importance sampling (SIS) smoother removes the m discontinuity structures of a discrete barrier one date at a time (a per-date survival change of measure in the Glasserman-Staum spirit), combined with a tailored path-generation method, under Black-Scholes and subordinated-BM (Variance Gamma) models. The abstract claims large variance reduction 'with improved rate of convergence' and greatly reduced effective dimension. Whether this is single- or multi-asset, and the fitted exponents, are unknown.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the most direct potential contradiction of C2 and is UNRESOLVED. If its tables show near n^-1 RQMC for multi-date discrete knock-outs, the claim 'smoothing methods tried fail for knock-outs' becomes 'the methods we tried fail; a published SIS+PGM smoother reportedly improves the rate'. The 2017-2019 He-Wang paper by the same group (F03) calls barrier gains 'moderate' because of cusps, which suggests the improvement is partial, but that is inference. Action before C2 is frozen: obtain the full text (library access) and extract its exponents and asset count. At minimum cite it and qualify C2 as limited to the smoothers actually executed. Not in the four designated files.

title: Numerical Smoothing with Hierarchical Adaptive Sparse Grids and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods for Efficient Option Pricing (with companion: Multilevel Monte Carlo with Numerical Smoothing for Robust and Efficient Computation of Probabilities and Densities, arXiv 2003.05708)
authors: Christian Bayer, Chiheb Ben Hammouda, Raul Tempone
year_and_status: 2111.01874: arXiv 2021-2022, published per arXiv comments (already in SCREENING_TABLE.md). 2003.05708: v1 12 Mar 2020, v4 2 Oct 2023; the repository's Utrecht copy is filename-coded as SIAM 22M1495718 (journal not verified).
what_it_does: Numerical smoothing: root-find the kink/jump location along one direction (Z1, from the Brownian bridge coarsest factor) and integrate that direction with 1-D quadrature, then apply ASGQ or RQMC (or MLMC in the companion) to the smoothed remainder. Remark 2.5 allows finitely many roots along the single direction. Remark 2.2 says the smoothing direction is fixed to Z1 and that path-dependent payoffs may need a linear combination of directions, which is left open. No barrier or knock-out example appears in either paper, per the pages inspected.
difference_from_our_paper: This is relevant to C2's scope and to plan item C5 ('multi-direction numerical smoothing'). The published method is single-direction and not demonstrated on discretely monitored barriers. It does not show knock-outs regaining n^-1, so it does not contradict C2. It also means a multi-direction smoother for knock-outs would be the project's own construction, not a published baseline, and must be described as such. new=false because 2111.01874 is already screened; the barrier-scope observation (Remarks 2.2/2.5) and the 2003.05708 companion are additions.

title: On the convergence rate of randomized quasi-Monte Carlo for discontinuous functions (with: Z. He, Quasi-Monte Carlo for discontinuous integrands with singularities along the boundary of the unit cube, Math. Comp. 2018)
authors: Zhijian He, Xiaoqun Wang (2015); Zhijian He (2018)
year_and_status: SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 53 (2015) 2488-2503, and Math. Comp. (2018) DOI 10.1090/mcom/3324. Both publisher pages were blocked (HTTP 403). Citations and the rate were verified from the author's own arXiv paper 1708.09512 (He, SINUM 2019), refs [11] and [13] and Sec. 4.
what_it_does: Gives upper bounds for scrambled-net RQMC on discontinuous integrands whose discontinuity boundary is not axis-aligned. As restated in He (arXiv 1708.09512, Sec. 1 and around eq. 4.1), the mean error is O(n^(-1/2-1/(4d-2)+eps)), which 'deteriorates quickly as the dimension d goes up'. He 2019 shows that conditioning (preintegration) restores O(n^(-1+eps)) for all ANOVA terms except the highest-order non-smooth one when a suitable monotone conditioning variable exists.
difference_from_our_paper: Provides the theoretical expectation for C2's knock-out exponents. For a knock-out integrand that stays discontinuous or kinked in d-1 = 47 or 415 non-aligned dimensions after conditioning, the guaranteed rate is essentially n^-0.5 (the bound exponent is about 0.505 at d=48). Our measured 0.48-0.63 exponents are therefore what the theory allows, not a surprise. These are upper bounds, not lower bounds, so they cannot show that no smoother reaches n^-1. C2 must remain empirical ('methods tried'). This also constrains C1: for knock-outs the relevant classical cost model is near-MC scaling with a smaller constant, so r is about 0.5-0.6, not r about 1. Not in the four designated files; 1708.09512 itself is already screened.

title: A Threshold for Quantum Advantage in Derivative Pricing
authors: Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Rajiv Krishnakumar, Guglielmo Mazzola, Nikitas Stamatopoulos, Stefan Woerner, William J. Zeng
what_it_does: End-to-end logical resource estimate for amplitude-estimation pricing of an autocallable and a TARF under GBM. It introduces re-parameterization loading and reports about 8k logical qubits and total T-depth 5.4x10^7 at 68% confidence. The conclusion assumes a 1-second pricing target and derives a required T-gate rate of about 10 MHz at a code distance supporting about 10^10 logical operations. Appendix A.4 describes classical autocallable pricing anecdotally ('five to ten seconds' with at least 40k MC paths); the classical side is not timed and uses plain MC, not QMC/RQMC.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the canonical finance threshold paper and already establishes the 'required logical clock rate for advantage' framing. Any claim that the requirements-frontier idea is new is pre-empted. Differences: (1) the classical side is an assumed 1-s target at 68% confidence against plain MC, whereas ours is timed RQMC with fitted rates and a 99%/10x contract; (2) autocallable/TARF, whereas ours is a discretely monitored basket knock-out with measured smoothing failure; (3) T-depth comes from hand-counted arithmetic, whereas ours is an emitted, basis-replayed compiled source with width; (4) no joint sensitivity factorial or calculator. Our 6.0x10^6 clean T-depth per oracle call is not comparable with their 5.4x10^7 total-algorithm T-depth without the call count. ADVERSARIAL POINT FOR C3/C4: their Table 1 / Sec. 4.2.3 contract already contains discretely monitored barrier logic on several assets (3-asset basket autocallable with a knock-in put over 20 barrier dates). Their Q operator is costed at T-depth 9.5k with 8k qubits (Sec. 4.2.3), and the payoff circuit at T-depth 3.2k (Sec. 5.1). Our generic emitted B4x12 knock-out source has 6.0x10^6 clean scheduled T-depth and 5.5x10^5 logical qubits, about 600x deeper for a comparably sized barrier structure. A referee will read much of C4's miss factor as compiler and arithmetic inefficiency (72-bit words, coherent Box-Muller, generic leaves) rather than an intrinsic requirement. The paper must place the Chakrabarti-style hand count as the optimistic end of the bracket; WHY_NO_ADVANTAGE.md already notes this for the 9.5x10^3 figure (still 13-65x too deep). A 'first compiled multi-asset barrier oracle' claim is defensible only as 'first emitted and basis-replayed', not first costed. new=false (R1 in PRIMARY_SOURCE_BIBLIOGRAPHY.md; screening table).

title: Derivative Pricing using Quantum Signal Processing
year_and_status: arXiv v1 26 Jul 2023, v2 16 Apr 2024; Quantum 8:1322 (2024)
what_it_does: Replaces reversible payoff arithmetic with QSP-encoded payoffs. The abstract reports about 16x fewer T-gates, about 4x fewer logical qubits and about 5x lower required logical clock rate than prior state of the art: 4.7k logical qubits and about 10^9 T-gates at a 45 MHz rate for advantage. The classical target is inherited from the threshold framing, not re-timed.
difference_from_our_paper: This sets the state-of-the-art quantum-favourable oracle cost for a finance payoff and must be a row in the frontier and oracle-family table (L6). The QSP route avoids the arithmetic that dominates our compiled knock-out source. Our frontier should therefore show where a QSP-class oracle (if it could encode a basket knock-out) would sit relative to D_max, rather than implying that our reversible-IR depth is the best achievable. Its classical side is not a measured RQMC comparator. new=false (N2 in PRIMARY_SOURCE_BIBLIOGRAPHY.md).

title: Quantum-accelerated multilevel Monte Carlo methods for stochastic differential equations in mathematical finance
authors: Dong An, Noah Linden, Jin-Peng Liu, Ashley Montanaro, Changpeng Shao, Jiasu Wang
year_and_status: arXiv v1 11 Dec 2020, revised 22 Jun 2021; Quantum 5:481 (2021)
what_it_does: Quantum versions of MLMC for SDE-based pricing (Black-Scholes, local volatility, Greeks, binomial). The abstract claims a quadratic speed-up over classical MLMC in query/sample-complexity terms with improved precision dependence. There is no timed classical comparator and no QMC/RQMC comparison on the abstract page.
difference_from_our_paper: This is the asymptotic complexity argument our paper takes as given and then prices out. Our C1 budget identity converts such a query-count advantage into a wall-clock depth budget against measured RQMC. Where classical RQMC reaches r about 1 (smooth payoffs), the quadratic gap in epsilon largely closes; for knock-outs (r about 0.5-0.6) it remains, but the constant-factor gap dominates (C4). No overlap with C2 or C4. new=false: named in SCREENING_TABLE.md ('cached An et al. QA-MLMC') and in WHY_NO_ADVANTAGE.md refs.

title: Efficient State Preparation for Quantum Amplitude Estimation
what_it_does: Per the abstract, proposes an approach to simplify QAE state preparation together with a circuit optimization technique; the mechanism details were not read beyond the abstract. It demonstrates numerical integration on hardware and Heston-model option pricing in simulation. The abstract states that state preparation that is too expensive can diminish the quadratic advantage.
difference_from_our_paper: An oracle-family entry for L6 (loading/state-preparation alternatives). It gives no logical resource totals against a timed classical comparator and no threshold. Our result quantifies how much such state-preparation savings would need to deliver (about 10^3-10^4x shallower oracles for the knock-out). Cite it in the oracle-family table as a loading-cost reduction whose effect on the knock-out budget is not established. Not in the four designated files.

title: Accelerating Python for Exotic Option Pricing (NVIDIA Technical Blog)
year_and_status: 19 Mar 2020; vendor technical blog, not peer reviewed
what_it_does: Prices a single-asset discretely monitored down-and-out Asian call (S0=120, K=110, B=100, sigma=0.35, T=1, 365 daily steps) with 8.192M pseudo-random (cuRAND MTGP32) MC paths on one V100 16 GB. Reported times: CUDA C++ 26.6 ms, CuPy RawKernel 29 ms, Numba-CUDA 65 ms, Numba CPU 32-core 2,340 ms, Numba CPU single-core 41,600 ms. The reported std. dev. at 8M paths is 0.0073 on a price of about $18.70. It also trains a neural-network surrogate (0.8 ms, 0.2 ms with TensorRT). This implies about 1.1x10^11 path-steps/s on a 2017-generation GPU.
difference_from_our_paper: A usable public anchor for the GPU factor g on our own payoff class (a discretely monitored Asian barrier). The same MC kernel is about 88x faster on one V100 than on a 32-core CPU via Numba (2,340/26.6), and about 35x even for Numba-CUDA. It is plain pseudo-random MC, single asset, vendor-authored and on 2020 hardware, so use it only as an order-of-magnitude anchor for g in {10, 100}, not a measured comparator for our RQMC estimator. Its throughput also shows the classical side can price a single-asset barrier to about $0.007 standard deviation in tens of milliseconds, which tightens D_max further if adopted. Not in the four designated files.

title: STAC-A2 reports: NVIDIA H100 PCIe (Sep 2023, 8 GPUs in HPE ProLiant XL675d Gen10 Plus) and Intel Xeon 6 CPU records (AWS EC2 c8i.metal-96xl, INTC251024, 14 Nov 2025; HPE ProLiant Compute XD230 with Xeon 6980P, INTC260430, 20 May 2026)
authors: STAC (Strategic Technology Analysis Center); vendor-sponsored audited reports
year_and_status: STAC news pages opened: docs.stacresearch.com/news/NVDA230721 (Sep 2023), stacresearch.com/news/intc251024 (Nov 2025), and stacresearch.com/news/stac-a2-on-hpe-proliant-compute-xd230-with-intel-xeon-6980p-processors-and-micron-mrdimms/ (May 2026). Full reports sit behind the STAC Vault and were not read.
what_it_does: STAC-A2 is an audited derivatives-risk benchmark (Heston-type multi-asset path-dependent MC with Greeks). 8x H100 PCIe (2023): baseline Greeks warm 8.9 ms, cold 38 ms; large Greeks warm 0.51 s, cold 1.85 s; up to 400 correlated assets; 3.1x10^8 paths in 10 min. 2x Xeon 6975P-C, AWS (2025): baseline Greeks cold 34.7 ms, then a record. HPE XD230 with Xeon 6980P (2026): cold 33.4 ms, a new cold record. The news pages give no CPU warm-baseline absolute time. The 2024 8x H100 SXM5 result (warm 7.40 ms) is already in SCREENING_TABLE.md.
difference_from_our_paper: This matters for the g anchor. On STAC-A2 cold baseline Greeks, a current 2-socket Xeon 6 server (33-35 ms) matches or beats the 2023 8-GPU H100 PCIe node (38 ms). The GPU advantage appears mainly in warm and large-problem runs, and the vendor-optimized CPU code is itself far stronger than naive CPU baselines. Therefore g should not be taken as 100x node-for-node from STAC-A2. A defensible statement is that audited node-level GPU/CPU ratios on STAC-A2 are modest and depend on warm/cold and problem size (exact warm CPU figures unknown here), while naive-CPU comparisons (F15) give about 10^2. Our CPU RQMC timing is itself 'strong CPU', so the frontier should carry g in {1, 10, 100} with this citation rather than a single g. The STAC-A2 family is already screened; these specific reports are new.

title: A Survey of Quantum Computing for Finance
authors: Herman et al. (full author list not re-verified in this session)
year_and_status: arXiv 2022 preprint (abstract page opened); a later journal version is not verified here
what_it_does: A broad survey of quantum algorithms for finance (simulation/Monte Carlo pricing, optimization, machine learning) and their feasibility on near-term devices. Per the abstract page inspected, it gives no concrete timeline or quantitative resource threshold for derivative pricing advantage.
difference_from_our_paper: Survey-level context only: it motivates derivative pricing as a candidate application but has no measured classical comparator, no depth budget and no knock-out analysis. It is useful as the standard survey citation in the introduction and does not affect C1-C7 novelty. Not in the four designated files.
